views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the Sept 24 5–10% retaliation in place and reopen talks only on equal footing, with no new purchase or structural commitments until Washington freezes the Jan 1, 2019 lift of List 3 from 10% to 25% and parks the threatened $267B phase-three list. Do not add further tariffs or qualitative measures now: remaining U.S. goods are too thin to match, and another move might give Trump a pretext to cover almost all remaining Chinese exports to the U.S. Use domestic demand support and a managed yuan to absorb the hit while testing whether a post-List-3 channel (Liu He / working-level) can buy time before January.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. Combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is now ~$250B after List 3 took effect at 10% on 24 Sept, with an already-announced step-up to 25% on 1 Jan 2019 (timeline 2018-09-17, 2018-09-24). That sits on top of the $50B at 25% (Lists 1–2) and earlier firm-level tech pressure (ZTE denial order 16 Apr; NDAA restrictions on Huawei/ZTE). The yuan has weakened about 9.5% since early April (DEXCHUS 6.28 → 6.8763 on 26 Sept), industrial production growth has slowed from 7.0% y/y in April to 5.8% in September, and reserves have slipped ~1.2%. Those are the +0.5-anchor ingredients: major export exposure, FX pressure, and national-champion targeting. They are not +1.0: seasonally adjusted merchandise exports were still rising into September, the discount rate is unchanged at 2.9%, reserves remain ~$3.11T, and the yuan move itself offsets a large part of the new 10% List 3 rate. Deutsche Bank-type estimates circulating before the decision date put a full escalation at only ~0.5pp of growth, with the U.S. about 12% of China’s exports. Action should stay near zero because China has already retaliated in kind ($3B on 232; matching $50B on 301; then 5–10% on ~$60B / 5,207 lines on 24 Sept) and has now tariffed most of the ~$130B it buys from the U.S. Further tariff or non-tariff escalation would be mostly symbolic and might trigger the $267B phase-three list Trump attached to any Chinese counter-move. Unilateral rollback or purchase concessions would repeat the 19 May joint statement that the White House abandoned ten days later (29 May). The correct stance is therefore negotiate without new commitments: keep the current retaliatory schedule, leave the door open after Mnuchin’s invitation, and use the 10%→25% window rather than walking into a broader export shock.
key_factors: List 3 ($200B at 10%) is live as of 24 Sept and is scheduled to rise to 25% on 1 Jan 2019, taking combined U.S. 301 coverage to ~$250B
China has already used most tariff ammunition (~$110B of ~$130B of U.S. goods) and cut planned List-3 rates to 5–10% rather than 25%
Trump has tied a further ~$267B list (nearly all remaining Chinese exports to the U.S.) to any additional Chinese retaliation
CNY has depreciated ~9.5% since April, offsetting much of the new 10% duty but raising financial-stability and capital-outflow risk if it overshoots
China IP growth is slowing (7.0% → 5.8% y/y) while overall exports and ~$3.11T reserves still show resilience, so the shock is material not existential
May 19 purchase-truce collapsed on May 29; talks are invited but the atmosphere is described as poisoned — so talks without new commitments, not concessions

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
CNY/USD from 6.2785 (2018-04-02) to 6.8763 (2018-09-26); +9.52% yuan depreciation over the window.
China industrial production index y/y slowed from 107.0 (Apr) to 105.8 (Sep).
China total reserves ex-gold ~$3.106T in Sep vs ~$3.144T in Apr; modest ~1.2% decline, still ample.
China SA merchandise exports still rising into Sep ($216.3B) vs Apr ($208.6B), so the tariff shock has not yet broken the export aggregate.

Trump warned that if China retaliated he would immediately pursue phase three — tariffs on approximately $267 billion of additional imports. China cut planned $60B retaliation rates to 5 and 10 percent from a previously proposed 5/10/20/25 schedule.
U.S. goods exports to China total only about $130 billion, so after the $60B list Beijing has tariffed most of what it buys and may have to look beyond tariffs to retaliate further.
